title: Festivals and everyday culture
job: Talk about what is happening around you
verifiedBy: Claude Opus 5 — LLM review, authorised by repo owner

rules.text: TWO CALENDARS run at once, and that is the real content of this module. The Gregorian months (yanāyir, dīsambir) are what a form and a bus timetable use; the hijrī months (muḥarram, ramaḍān, shawwāl) are what a festival is fixed to. The hijrī year is shorter, so ramaḍān walks backwards through the Gregorian year by about eleven days each time — which is why "when is Eid" has no fixed answer, and why a diary alone will not tell you.

kull heads an IḌĀFA, L3-M2's construct in the field, and the ARTICLE flips the meaning. kull yawm is "every day"; kull al-yawm is "the whole day". kull sana is "every year"; kull as-sana is "the whole year". One al-, two different sentences.

The greetings are frozen and are learnt whole, exactly as L1-M2's alḥamdu lillāh was: kull ʿām wa antum bi-khayr (said at any annual occasion), ʿīd mubārak (at the Eid itself), mabrūk (for anything congratulable). None of them is taken apart for grammar, and none of them needs to be.

naḥtafil takes bi- for what is celebrated: naḥtafil bi-al-ʿīd. That is M6's ashʿuru bi- pattern again — a verb reaching its object through a preposition where English needs none — and the third time this level has asked for it.

Broken plurals (aʿyād, hadāyā, ʿuṭal, aʿwām) sit in their singular's forms as VOCABULARY. Do not look for a rule: a calendar module is where you meet the most of them at once, and each is learnt as its own word.

sentences.cue: We celebrate the Eid every year

words.note: We celebrate. It reaches its object through bi-, like M6's ashʿuru: naḥtafil bi-al-ʿīd. aḥtafil is I, yaḥtafil is he.
A festival, and with the article the Eid. ʿ is a moon letter: al-ʿīd. Plural aʿyād, broken, taken as vocabulary.
Year. s is a sun letter: as-sana. Plural sanawāt. ʿām is its twin and means the same thing.

sentences.trap: English celebrates something directly. Arabic celebrates WITH it, and the bi- is not optional — the third verb this level has handed you that needs a preposition English does not.
sentences.sound: naḥ-TA-fil bil-ʿEED kull SA-na — the ḥ is breathy and the ʿ is a squeeze.

variations.cue: I celebrate the Eid every year
variations.changed: who: naḥtafil → aḥtafil

variations.cue: We celebrate the Eid in Shawwal
variations.changed: how often → in which month

mistake.why: The bi- has been dropped because English does not need one. naḥtafil bi-al-ʿīd — the verb only reaches its object through the preposition.

sentences.usage: The plain statement of a family's year, and the answer to "what do you do at Eid?".
sentences.mnemonic: You celebrate WITH the festival, not the festival.

sentences.cue: Happy new year / many happy returns

words.cue: may you be well every year
words.note: One frozen greeting, learnt whole like alḥamdu lillāh. Said at any yearly occasion — Eid, a birthday, a new year, hijrī or Gregorian.
Year — sana's twin, and the one the greeting froze around. Plural aʿwām, broken.

sentences.trap: Do not translate this and do not take it apart. The antum inside it is a plural "you" the ladder has not taught, and the phrase is one unit — treat it as a single word with five spaces in it.
sentences.sound: kull ʿAAM wa an-TUM bi-KHAYR — said fast, almost as one word, with the stress landing on KHAYR.

variations.cue: Many happy returns (to one man)
variations.changed: the everyday version: ʿām → sana, antum → anta

variations.cue: Blessed Eid
variations.changed: the occasion — the greeting for the Eid itself

mistake.why: The wa is structural, not decorative: it joins the two halves of the wish. Dropped, the phrase stops being the greeting and becomes a flat statement.

sentences.usage: Said and answered on every annual occasion, and answered with the same words back.
sentences.mnemonic: Five words, one greeting, no parts.

sentences.display: ʿīd mubārak, kull sana wa anta bi-khayr
sentences.script: عيد مبارك، كل سنة وأنت بخير
sentences.literal: Festival blessed, every year and you in-good

words.note: The Eid greeting, frozen whole. Said on the day itself and for two or three days after it.
Congratulations — for a job, a baby, a car, a pass. Not tied to the calendar, and said on its own.

sentences.trap: Three greetings, three occasions: ʿīd mubārak for the Eid, kull ʿām wa antum bi-khayr for anything yearly, mabrūk for a piece of good news. They are not interchangeable and none of them is a translation of "happy".
sentences.sound: ʿEED mu-BAA-rak — a clear pause at the comma, then the second greeting at speed.

variations.cue: Blessed Eid
variations.changed: the second half dropped — it stands alone perfectly well

variations.cue: Congratulations!
variations.changed: the occasion: a festival → any piece of good news

mistake.why: mabrūk congratulates a person on something they did or received. A festival arrives for everybody, so the word for it is ʿīd mubārak.

sentences.usage: The doorway exchange at Eid, said twice over before anyone sits down.
sentences.mnemonic: mubārak for the day, mabrūk for the news.

sentences.cue: Ramadan is a month in the hijri calendar

words.note: The ninth hijrī month, the month of fasting. shahr ramaḍān is the full name — an iḍāfa, L3-M2's two nouns touching.
Calendar. t is a sun letter: at-taqwīm. Which one you mean has to be said, because two are in daily use.
Of the hijrī calendar, counted from the emigration to Medina. Its year is about eleven days shorter than the Gregorian one.
Of the Gregorian calendar — the one on a form or a bus timetable. Both dates are often printed side by side.

sentences.trap: Ramadan has no fixed Gregorian date and never will: the hijrī year is shorter, so it moves back about eleven days each time. Anyone asking you "when is Ramadan next year" is asking a real question, not a lazy one.
sentences.sound: SHAHR ra-ma-ḌAAN fit-taq-WEEM al-HIJ-ree — the ḍ is the heavy d, said with the jaw low.

variations.cue: January is in the Gregorian calendar
variations.changed: which calendar, and which month belongs to it

variations.cue: Ramadan comes before Shawwal
variations.changed: the calendar named → the order inside it

mistake.why: This pins a hijrī month to a Gregorian one, which cannot be done. Ramadan falls in a different Gregorian month every few years — that is the whole point of two calendars.

sentences.usage: The one sentence that explains why the dates on a wall calendar and the dates people live by disagree.
sentences.mnemonic: Two calendars, one sky, eleven days of drift.

sentences.cue: The Eid is in Shawwal, after Ramadan

words.note: The tenth hijrī month, the one that opens with the Eid. The doubled w is held: shaw-WAAL.
The first hijrī month, where the hijrī year begins — the equivalent of January in the other calendar.

sentences.trap: There is no verb here, and none is needed: a date is stated the way a price was in M8, by putting the two facts next to each other.

variations.cue: The festival is in Muharram
variations.changed: which month — the hijri year's first

variations.cue: The holiday is after Ramadan
variations.changed: what falls there: the Eid → the holiday around it

mistake.why: The huwa is an English "is" that Arabic never asked for. al-ʿīd fī shawwāl is a complete sentence exactly as it stands.

sentences.usage: How the year gets explained to a visitor, and how a colleague tells you when the office will be empty.
sentences.mnemonic: Ramadan ends, Shawwal opens, the Eid is the door.

sentences.cue: I have a holiday in January

words.note: Time off work — a day, a week, a fortnight. Plural ʿuṭal, broken. Held by ʿindī, like everything else you have.
January, in the Gregorian calendar. Month names take no article and never change shape.
December. Like yanāyir, a borrowed name said close to how it looks — and like it, never carries al-.

sentences.trap: A month name takes no article: fī yanāyir, never fī al-yanāyir. It is one of the few nouns on this ladder that refuses al- outright.

variations.cue: I have a holiday in December
variations.changed: which month: yanāyir → dīsambir

variations.cue: I have a holiday after the Eid
variations.changed: a Gregorian month → the festival it hangs off

mistake.why: Month names are already definite. fī yanāyir, with nothing in front of it.

sentences.usage: Said when someone asks about your year, and the sentence that starts every plan to travel.

words.note: A present. Plural hadāyā, broken and worth memorising on its own — it is what a shop window is labelled at Eid.

sentences.trap: hadiyya is indefinite here, with no al-, because it is a present and not the present. Arabic marks that by leaving the article off, and English marks it with "a" — one word against nothing.
sentences.sound: ish-ta-RAY-tu ha-DIY-ya al-YAWM — the doubled y is held.

variations.cue: I bought a present for the Eid
variations.changed: what it is for, with L1-M9's li-

variations.cue: I bought the presents today
variations.changed: one gift → the broken plural, hadāyā

mistake.why: Not wrong, but it says "THE present" — the one you and your listener both already have in mind. For a present nobody has mentioned yet, leave the al- off.

sentences.usage: The everyday past-tense sentence of festival week, said in every shop queue.

sentences.cue: The party is at the house on Friday evening

words.note: A party or a formal gathering — a wedding, a graduation, a concert. Regular plural ḥaflāt. Same root as naḥtafil.
The celebrating itself — the maṣdar of naḥtafil, where ḥafla is the event you attend. Same root, different job.

sentences.trap: masāʾ al-jumʿa is an iḍāfa, "the evening of the Friday", and it needs no preposition. But fī al-bayt does need its fī — the construct only replaces "of", never "in".

variations.cue: The party is at the restaurant
variations.changed: where: al-bayt → al-maṭʿam

variations.cue: The celebration is at the house on Friday evening
variations.changed: the event → the celebrating, al-iḥtifāl

mistake.display: al-ḥafla fī al-bayt fī masāʾ al-jumʿa
mistake.script: الحفلة في البيت في مساء الجمعة
mistake.why: The second fī is the English "on" carried across. masāʾ al-jumʿa already says "on Friday evening" by itself.

sentences.usage: The invitation as it actually arrives — place, then time, no verb anywhere.
sentences.mnemonic: fī for the place, nothing at all for the time.

sentences.display: al-iḥtifāl al-kabīr fī al-awwal min yanāyir
sentences.script: الاحتفال الكبير في الأول من يناير
sentences.cue: The big celebration is on the first of January
sentences.literal: The-celebration the-big in the-first from January

words.note: The first. A date is al-awwal min + the month. al-ūlā is its feminine — the ordinals for clock hours were L2-M6's.

sentences.trap: A date is built with min, not fī: al-awwal min yanāyir, "the first FROM January". English says "of", Arabic says "from", and neither is an iḍāfa here.

variations.cue: The celebration is on the first of Muharram
variations.changed: which calendar's first — the hijri new year

variations.cue: The holiday is on the first of December
variations.changed: what falls on the date, and which month

mistake.why: Heard in speech, but the careful form keeps both pieces: al-awwal min yanāyir. Write it that way on anything anyone else will read.

sentences.usage: How a date is said aloud when it matters — an invitation, an appointment, a deadline.

sentences.display: kull yawm ʿamal, wa kull al-yawm ʿuṭla
sentences.script: كل يوم عمل، وكل اليوم عطلة
sentences.cue: Every day is work — and the whole day is a holiday
sentences.literal: Every day work, and all the-day holiday

words.note: The minimal pair of the module: kull yawm is every day, kull al-yawm is the whole day. The al- on the second noun is the only difference.

sentences.trap: Two phrases, one word apart, and they mean opposite things. If you hear kull and reach for "every" without checking the next word for al-, you will get this backwards about half the time.
sentences.sound: kull YAWM ʿA-mal, wa kull al-YAWM ʿUṬ-la — a real pause at the comma, and the al- said clearly.

variations.cue: Every year, a party
variations.changed: the unit: yawm → sana, and no article, so still every

variations.cue: The whole year is a holiday
variations.changed: the article added — every year becomes the whole year

mistake.why: If you meant "work every day", the al- has changed it to "the whole day is work" — true of one day, not of your life. kull yawm ʿamal is the one you wanted.

sentences.usage: The pair to say out loud twice, because it is the level's sharpest one-letter difference.
sentences.mnemonic: No al-, every. With al-, the whole.
